nameStory: The Acadian redfish gets its name from its vibrant reddish-orange coloration that makes it stand out against the deep, dark waters where it lives. The 'Acadian' part refers to the historical Acadia region of northeastern North America, which encompasses much of its Atlantic range. It's also called Atlantic redfish or rockfish, reflecting both its ocean home and its rocky bottom habitat preferences.
description: The Acadian redfish is a stocky, deep-bodied marine fish with a striking red to orange coloration that can range from bright scarlet to more muted reddish-brown. These fish have large, prominent eyes adapted for life in deeper waters and a somewhat compressed body shape typical of rockfishes. They typically grow to about 12-20 inches long, with a robust build and spiny fins characteristic of their scorpionfish family. You'll find them in the cold, deep waters off New England's coast, usually at depths where most recreational anglers rarely venture.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Vibrant red to orange body coloration that feels slightly rough to the touch due to small scales, ranging from bright scarlet in younger fish to deeper reddish-brown in older individuals

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, laterally compressed body that feels solid and muscular, with a distinctly stocky profile that tapers toward the tail

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Sharp, spiny dorsal fin that can prick your finger if handled carelessly, with the spiny portion clearly separated from the softer rear section

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Unusually large, prominent eyes that feel slightly bulging to the touch, an adaptation for seeing in the dim light of deeper waters

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth position with a slightly protruding lower jaw, opening wide enough to engulf substantial prey

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deep, cold Atlantic waters typically 100-600 feet down, over rocky bottoms and slopes along the continental shelf

habitat: Acadian redfish live in the deep, cold waters of the North Atlantic off New England's coast, typically at depths of 100-600 feet where the water temperature stays consistently cool year-round. They prefer areas with rocky bottoms, underwater ledges, and the continental shelf edge where they can find shelter and abundant food. You're most likely to encounter them if you're deep-sea fishing or if one occasionally gets caught in deeper commercial fishing operations.

seasonality.spring: Redfish remain in deep waters during spring, with some movement toward slightly shallower areas as water temperatures stabilize. This is when they're most actively feeding after winter.
seasonality.summer: They stay in their preferred deep, cool waters even as surface temperatures warm, making summer the most predictable time to find them at consistent depths.
seasonality.fall: Breeding season occurs in fall, when females give birth to live young (they don't lay eggs). Adults may show slightly more vibrant coloration during this reproductive period.
seasonality.winter: Fish remain in deep waters where temperatures stay stable, though they may move to slightly deeper areas to avoid any temperature fluctuations from winter storms above.

funFact: Acadian redfish don't lay eggs like most fish — instead, females give birth to thousands of tiny, fully-formed live babies that look like miniature versions of their parents, swimming away immediately after birth!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other red-colored fish, but the Acadian redfish's deep-water habitat and large eyes set it apart from shallow-water species. Remember: if you caught it in deep, cold water and it has huge eyes and bright red coloring, you've likely found a redfish.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'rockfish' in some areas, this species is completely different from the striped bass that East Coast anglers also call 'rockfish' — the names are confusing but refer to totally different fish families. The Acadian redfish is also sometimes marketed as 'ocean perch' in restaurants, though it's not closely related to freshwater perch.
compareHints: Since it's the only Sebastes species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other members of the scorpionfish family by looking for the characteristic spiny fins and robust body shape. However, most other scorpionfishes in our region are smaller and have more mottled coloration rather than the solid red-orange of the Acadian redfish. The large eyes and deep-water habitat also distinguish it from coastal scorpionfishes.
